threats.title: Reused passwords let attackers sign in as Email provider
threats.description: Email provider authenticates over the public internet. Attackers try passwords leaked from other services against it, and anyone who reuses a password is exposed even though nothing in this system was breached.
threats.status_reason: The Reminder worker signs in to the provider with an API key issued per deployment, never with a password a person types, so there is no password to reuse.

threats.title: Stolen credentials let an attacker act as Email provider
threats.description: Email provider proves who it is with a credential such as a password, key or token. If that credential is stolen, leaked or guessed, the attacker is indistinguishable from the real entity until someone notices.

threats.title: Email provider can deny having done something
threats.description: If the system keeps no trustworthy record of what Email provider asked for, the entity can later claim it never did, and the system cannot show otherwise. That matters most for orders, approvals, deletions and payments.

threats.title: Reused passwords let attackers sign in as Note taker
threats.description: Note taker authenticates over the public internet. Attackers try passwords leaked from other services against it, and anyone who reuses a password is exposed even though nothing in this system was breached.

threats.title: Stolen credentials let an attacker act as Note taker
threats.description: Note taker proves who it is with a credential such as a password, key or token. If that credential is stolen, leaked or guessed, the attacker is indistinguishable from the real entity until someone notices.

threats.title: Note taker can deny having done something
threats.description: If the system keeps no trustworthy record of what Note taker asked for, the entity can later claim it never did, and the system cannot show otherwise. That matters most for orders, approvals, deletions and payments.

threats.title: A stolen session lets an attacker act as a signed-in user of Notes API
threats.description: Once a user has signed in, Notes API recognises them by a session credential. Anyone who obtains that credential, for example through a script injected into a page, a leaked log line or a stolen device, can act as the user until the session ends.

threats.title: Another program can pose as Notes API to the components that call it
threats.description: Components that call Notes API need to be sure they are talking to the real one. If an attacker can take over its name or address, or sit on the path to it, they can answer in its place and collect what callers send.

threats.title: Crafted input from the internet can change what Notes API does
threats.description: Notes API takes input from the public internet. Anyone can send it data shaped to be misread: an oversized value, a wrong type, or text that looks like a command or query. If the process trusts that input, the attacker decides what it does.

threats.title: The code, dependencies or configuration of Notes API can be altered
threats.description: An attacker who can change what Notes API runs gets everything the process can do. The route can be a poisoned dependency, a tampered build or image, or a changed configuration or environment variable.

threats.title: Access to sensitive data through Notes API leaves no trail
threats.description: Notes API handles sensitive data. If reads, exports and changes of that data are not recorded with who did them, a leak or a misuse cannot be traced, and a person who misused their access can deny it.

threats.title: Actions taken through Notes API cannot be reconstructed later
threats.description: Without a record of security-relevant events, nobody can say afterwards who signed in, who changed what or what an attacker did. Notes API may do the right thing and still be unable to prove it.

threats.title: A signed-in user may read someone else's data through Notes API
threats.description: Notes API knows who the caller is, but knowing who someone is does not say which records they may see. If it hands back whatever record is asked for, a signed-in user can read other people's data by changing an identifier in a request.

threats.title: Notes API may reveal its internals in error messages
threats.description: Detailed errors help developers and attackers alike. Stack traces, query text, file paths and version numbers in a response show an attacker how Notes API is built and where to push.

threats.title: Notes API may write sensitive data into logs, metrics or traces
threats.description: Logs are copied, indexed, shipped and read by many people and tools. If Notes API writes sensitive values into them, such as passwords, tokens, personal data or request bodies, the data ends up in places with much weaker protection than the system it came from.

threats.title: Shared note link can be guessed
threats.description: A note can be shared by link. If the link is short or predictable, someone who was never given it can open the note.

threats.title: Anyone on the internet can overwhelm Notes API
threats.description: Notes API accepts work from the public internet. Without limits, a flood of requests, a few very expensive ones or a slow connection held open on purpose can use up its CPU, memory or connections and shut out real users.

threats.title: Notes API stops working when something it depends on fails
threats.description: Notes API relies on other components such as databases, queues and other services. If one of them is slow or down and the process waits for it without a limit, requests pile up and the failure spreads.

threats.title: A signed-in user can reach functions in Notes API that are meant for others
threats.description: Notes API requires callers to sign in, but being signed in is not the same as being allowed. If it does not check permissions for each function, an ordinary user may reach administrative or other users' functions by calling them directly.

threats.title: Input from the internet could make Notes API run an attacker's code
threats.description: Notes API is reachable from the internet. If it evaluates input as code, deserializes untrusted data, handles uploaded files unsafely or uses a vulnerable dependency, an attacker can make it run their code and gain whatever the process itself can do.

threats.title: A user or service on the network could change data in Attachment bucket without permission
threats.description: Attachment bucket is not exposed to the internet, but every account and service that can reach it is a way to change what it holds. Shared administrative credentials and wide write permissions turn any single mistake or compromise into corrupted data.

threats.title: Backups of Attachment bucket can be altered, so a restore brings back bad data
threats.description: A backup is only useful if it holds what was really there. If someone can change or replace the copies of Attachment bucket, a restore after an incident reinstates the attacker's version, or fails when it is needed most.

threats.title: Changes to Attachment bucket cannot be traced to whoever made them
threats.description: If Attachment bucket keeps only its current contents, nobody can tell afterwards who changed a record, when, or what it said before. A wrong or malicious change cannot be attributed and cannot easily be undone.

threats.title: Reads of sensitive data in Attachment bucket leave no record
threats.description: Attachment bucket stores sensitive data. If reads are not logged, a leak cannot be traced to an account or a time, and anyone with access can look without being accountable.

threats.title: Copies of Attachment bucket, such as backups and exports, may be less protected than the original
threats.description: Sensitive data in Attachment bucket does not stay in one place: it is copied into backups, exports, replicas and test environments. Each copy is often guarded less well than the store itself, and any one of them can leak the lot.

threats.title: Sensitive data in Attachment bucket can be read from disks, snapshots or stolen media
threats.description: Attachment bucket stores sensitive data without encryption at rest. Anyone who gets hold of the underlying disk, a snapshot, a backup file or a decommissioned drive can read it directly, bypassing every access control in the application.

threats.title: Too many people or services can read sensitive data in Attachment bucket
threats.description: Over time, more accounts and services are granted access to Attachment bucket than need it. Each extra reader widens the chance of a leak by mistake, by compromise or by someone looking at what they should not.

threats.title: Attachment bucket can run out of space or capacity
threats.description: If nothing limits how much can be written to Attachment bucket, one runaway job, one noisy customer or one attacker can fill it. When it is full, writes fail and everything that depends on it stops.

threats.title: Data in Attachment bucket can be deleted or corrupted, taking the system down with it
threats.description: A mistaken command, a bad release or an attacker with write access can delete or overwrite the data in Attachment bucket. The system is then unusable until the data is back, if it can be.

threats.title: A user or service on the network could change data in Notes database without permission

threats.title: Backups of Notes database can be altered, so a restore brings back bad data

threats.status_reason: The cloud provider keeps versioned backups that the team’s own accounts cannot overwrite. Accepted until the quarterly restore test is automated, planned for next quarter.

threats.title: Changes to Notes database cannot be traced to whoever made them

threats.status_reason: Notes are personal and not shared, so who changed a row is rarely in doubt. Accepted until the audit log planned for version 2 is built.

threats.title: Notes database can run out of space or capacity
threats.description: If nothing limits how much can be written to Notes database, one runaway job, one noisy customer or one attacker can fill it. When it is full, writes fail and everything that depends on it stops.

threats.title: A captured message from Notes API to Attachment bucket can be sent again
threats.description: Attachment upload and download is authenticated, but authentication proves who sent a message, not that it is fresh. Someone who captures a valid message, for example a payment or a command, can send it again and Attachment bucket will accept it a second time.

threats.title: Data crossing a trust boundary into Attachment bucket may carry content that corrupts it
threats.description: Attachment upload and download brings data from outside a trust boundary straight toward Attachment bucket, a data store. Content that is malformed or crafted to be misread, such as injected query fragments, oversized values or unexpected structure, can corrupt what is stored.

threats.title: Notes API can flood Attachment bucket with messages across a trust boundary
threats.description: Attachment upload and download crosses a trust boundary. The sending side is less trusted than the receiving side, so it can send more than Attachment bucket can handle, by mistake or on purpose, and crowd out other work.

threats.description: Reads due reminders carries data from Reminder worker to Notes database without encryption, and the connection leaves one trust zone for another. Anyone on the path between the zones can modify the data before it arrives, and neither end can tell.

threats.description: Reads due reminders carries data from Reminder worker to Notes database without encryption, and the connection leaves one trust zone for another. Anyone on the network path between the zones can read it.

threats.description: Schedules reminders carries data from Notes API to Reminder worker without encryption. Both ends sit in the same trust zone, but a compromised machine or device on that network can still alter the data on its way.

threats.description: Schedules reminders carries data from Notes API to Reminder worker without encryption. Both ends are in the same trust zone, but anyone or anything that can see that network's traffic, such as a compromised machine or a misplaced tap, can read what passes.

mitigations.description: Alert on sign-ins from unusual places, times or volumes.
Prefer credentials that are hard to steal and easy to revoke, such as short-lived tokens or hardware-backed keys, over long-lived shared secrets.
Rotate credentials on a schedule and immediately after a suspected leak, and make revocation quick.
Store credentials in a secrets manager and keep them out of source code, logs and chat.
For actions that matter, keep evidence the party cannot dispute, such as a signed request or a confirmation they received.
Keep a tamper-resistant record of what each external party did: who, what, when and from where.
Keep these records for as long as disputes can arise.
Alert the owner on sign-ins from new places or devices.
Offer or require a second factor.
Reject passwords that appear in known breach lists when they are set.
Throttle failed sign-ins per account and per source address, without locking the real owner out.

Protect service discovery and name resolution against tampering.
Every request body is checked against a schema before it is used; contract tests send malformed bodies.

Limit request rates per client, and cap request size, concurrency and processing time.
Put a gateway, content delivery network or load balancer in front that can absorb and shed load.
Set a cost ceiling on any automatic scaling.
